About this simulation

On screen
Left: the energy per electron against the radius R, 0 to 20 000 km. The kinetic energy EK is dashed, the gravitational energy Egrav is dotted and their sum E is the solid accent curve. A bright marker sits on E at the star's radius, with a dotted line dropping to the radius axis. Right: the star on a dark sky, drawn to scale on a frame reaching 20 000 km from its centre, beside a disc the size of the Earth.
Controls
The mass slider sets M from 0.60 to 2.00 M☉; the chips and the number box beside it set an exact mass. The regime chooses non-relativistic electrons (energy p2/2me) or ultra-relativistic electrons (energy pc). Each change starts the marker again at the non-relativistic minimum for the current mass; in the ultra-relativistic regime it then moves at 4000 km per second of screen time, a display choice with no physical meaning.
Measured
All energies come from the uniform-sphere model with μe = 2, divided by the number of electrons: M in M☉, R at the marker in km and in Earth radii (6371 km), the mean kinetic energy per electron in keV, and the ratio EK/|Egrav| at the marker, all in the Readouts panel of the sidebar.
Model
A uniform sphere at T = 0 with μe = 2, its electrons taken as wholly non-relativistic or wholly ultra-relativistic. Real white dwarfs pass smoothly from one regime to the other as their mass grows. The limiting mass of this estimate, 1.72 M☉, lies above the true Chandrasekhar mass, 1.44 M☉, because a real white dwarf is centrally condensed rather than uniform.

Guided Inquiry

1 · The two energies at each end

Choose the non-relativistic regime and set the mass to 0.6 M☉. Before looking at the total-energy curve, predict which of the two energies has the larger size at very small radii and which at very large radii. Then compare the dashed and dotted curves near the left and right edges of the plot.

2 · A heavier white dwarf

Keep the non-relativistic regime and the mass at 0.6 M☉, and read the radius and the ratio EK/|Egrav| at the minimum. Before moving the slider, predict what happens to the radius of the minimum when the mass is raised to 1.2 M☉. Then raise the mass and watch the marker and the star panel.

3 · Energy per electron

Keep the non-relativistic regime and raise the mass to 2.0 M☉. Before reading the readout, predict what the mean kinetic energy per electron at the minimum tells you about this model, given that the rest energy of an electron is 511 keV. Then read it.

4 · Relativistic electrons

Set the mass to 1.0 M☉ and switch to the ultra-relativistic regime. Before watching the marker, predict what the total-energy curve looks like and what the star does.

5 · Finding the limiting mass

Keep the ultra-relativistic regime and watch the readout of EK/|Egrav|. Before moving the slider, predict what happens as the mass is raised slowly from 1.0 to 2.0 M☉. Then raise it, or type masses into the box, and find the mass at which the behaviour changes.

6 · What you found

With energy p2/2me the electrons' kinetic energy goes as 1/R2 and always beats gravity's −1/R at small radii, so every mass has a minimum, at R ∝ M−1/3, with EK = ½|Egrav|. Heavier stars push the electrons to relativistic energies; with energy pc both terms go as 1/R and there is no minimum: the star expands below the limiting mass and collapses above it. This uniform sphere puts the limit at 1.72 M☉; a real, centrally condensed white dwarf reaches it at 1.44 M☉, the Chandrasekhar mass.

The Physics

The Energy of a White Dwarf · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

A white dwarf has no fuel left and is held up by degenerate electrons. This sim treats it as a uniform sphere and plots the energy per electron against the radius R, to show where the star settles.

What you'll learn

  • What kinetic energy and gravity each add to the energy per electron.
  • Where the total energy is lowest, and how that radius depends on the mass.
  • What changes when the electrons are ultra-relativistic.
  • How that sets a limiting mass.
The sim's two views: the energy curves and the star beside the Earth.

What's on screen

  • Solid curve: the total energy per electron, E, against R from 0 to 20 000 km, with a bright marker at the star's radius.
  • Dashed curve: the kinetic energy of the electrons, EK.
  • Dotted curve: the gravitational energy, Egrav.
  • Right panel: the star drawn to scale, beside a disc the size of the Earth (6371 km).
  • Readouts, in the sidebar: M, R, R/R⊕, mean kinetic energy, EK/|Egrav|.
See itLook at the two views and the Readouts panel. Watch for: the three curves at left, the star beside the Earth at right, and the five readouts in the sidebar.

Every energy is the model's value divided by the number of electrons, in keV. The model has μe = 2 fixed.

03

The star is a uniform sphere of nuclei and degenerate electrons

The notes' estimate (section 5.1) treats the star as a uniform sphere of mass M and radius R. It holds Ne = M/(μemH) electrons, with μe = 2 for carbon and oxygen, which have two nucleons per electron.

The nuclei carry nearly all the mass; the electrons carry the kinetic energy.

The electrons are degenerate: the exclusion principle gives them large energies even at zero temperature, so they supply the kinetic energy EK. The sphere also has a gravitational energy Egrav, which is negative. The thermal energy of the nuclei is small and left out. The star settles at the radius where EK + Egrav is lowest, and the sim divides each energy by Ne, so every curve is in keV per electron.

See itOpen the sim at 0.60 M☉, non-relativistic, and look at the star. Watch for: the star drawn a little larger than the Earth disc: R = 8481 km, 1.33 Earth radii.
04

Kinetic energy wins at small radii, gravity at large radii

Squeezing degenerate electrons into a smaller sphere raises their Fermi momentum as 1/R, so their energy goes as 1/R² (5.10). A uniform sphere has Egrav going as 1/R (5.11). Here C1 collects (3/10)(9π/4)2/3ħ²Ne5/3/me:

Eqs. (5.10) and (5.11), per star. The 1/R² term is the larger in size at small R, the 1/R term at large R.
0.60 M☉, non-relativistic. The sum is lowest at 8481 km.

The sum E = C1/R² − C2/R is positive and steep at small R, negative at large R, and has one lowest point. Setting dE/dR = 0 gives the radius there (the stable equilibrium), and the virial theorem comes with it:

The minimum. At R0, EK is exactly half |Egrav|.
Key idea. The star's size is where the two terms balance: EK/|Egrav| = 0.5000 there.
See itOpen the sim at 0.60 M☉, non-relativistic, and look at the marker. Watch for: the marker at the lowest point of the solid curve, R = 8481 km, with the dashed curve above it and the dotted curve below.
05

A heavier white dwarf is smaller, and its electrons carry more energy

C1 grows as Ne5/3 and C2 as M², so R0 = 2C1/C2 falls as M−1/3 (5.12), and M R03 is the same for every white dwarf of this composition:

Eq. (5.12), the minimum radius. A stronger field squeezes the electrons harder before their pressure balances it.
R0 against mass: 8481 km at 0.60 M☉, 6732 km at 1.20 and 5678 km at 2.00.

Squeezing costs energy. The mean kinetic energy per electron at the minimum goes as M4/3.

Mean kinetic energy per electron at the minimum.

At 2.00 M☉ it is 293 keV, over half the electron's rest energy of 511 keV. Then p²/2me is no longer a good energy: the electrons are becoming relativistic.

See itRaise the mass from 0.60 to 2.00 M☉, non-relativistic. Watch for: R falling from 8481 to 6732 km (at 1.20) and 5678 km, while the mean kinetic energy climbs from 58.9 to 148.3 and 293.1 keV.
06

Ultra-relativistic electrons leave no minimum

For electrons at nearly the speed of light the energy is pc, and the kinetic energy becomes (5.13) the same power of R as gravity:

Eq. (5.13), and the total. Both terms go as 1/R.

The total (C3 − C2)/R then has no lowest point at any radius. If C3 > C2 it is positive and falls as R grows, so the star expands until its electrons are no longer ultra-relativistic. At 1.00 M☉, C3/C2 = EK/|Egrav| = 1.4351 at every radius, and at 0.60 M☉ it is 2.0174.

At 1.00 M☉ the total is positive and falls as R grows; at 2.00 M☉ it is negative and falls as R shrinks.

The sim starts the marker at the non-relativistic minimum and sends it in the direction the energy pushes. Its speed is a display choice.

See itSet 1.00 M☉, switch to ultra-relativistic and press Play. Watch for: the ratio reading 1.4351 wherever the marker is, and the marker running out to larger R.
07

The ratio falls through 1 at 1.72 solar masses

C3 goes as M4/3 and C2 as M², so C3/C2 goes as M−2/3. It equals 1 at the Chandrasekhar mass of this model (5.14), and the electron mass does not appear in it:

Eq. (5.14). For μe = 2 it gives 1.7192 M☉.
C3/C2 against mass: 2.017 at 0.60, 1.435 at 1.00, 1 at 1.72 and 0.904 at 2.00 M☉.

Above 1.72 M☉ the ratio is below 1, the total is negative, and it falls without limit as R shrinks: no pressure of the electrons stops the collapse.

The notes call the estimate about 1.7 M☉ and give the exact value, from the np = 3 Lane–Emden polytrope, as about 1.4 M☉ (1.44 M☉ more precisely). They are two models, not a disagreement.

See itSet ultra-relativistic at 1.00 M☉, press Play, then raise the mass to 2.00. Watch for: the ratio falling from 1.4351 through 1 near 1.72 M☉ to 0.9041, and the marker turning inward.
08

Where it matters

  • Sirius B. The notes give a mass of about 1.0 M☉ and a radius of about 0.008 R⊙, a little less than the Earth's. At 1.00 M☉ the sim reads 7153 km, 1.12 Earth radii: the right order, as a uniform sphere is only an estimate.
  • The typical white dwarf. The most common mass is about 0.6 M☉, where the sim reads 8481 km, a little larger than the Earth (notes: about 8.5 × 106 m).
  • A mass limit. No white dwarf can exceed the limiting mass; the masses measured in binaries are all below about 1.4 M☉.
Go deeper: joining the two limits

The sim shows the two limits only. The full radius against mass comes from the same minimisation with the energy √(p²c² + me²c⁴) − mec² (notes, Fig. 71). It follows R ∝ M−1/3 at small mass, and R falls to zero as M approaches the limit, because the electrons become ultra-relativistic throughout.

09

Summary

In one line. A white dwarf's radius is where the total energy per electron, from degenerate electrons and gravity, is lowest.
  • Non-relativistic: E = C1/R² − C2/R, lowest at R0 = 2C1/C2 ∝ M−1/3, with EK/|Egrav| = 0.5.
  • R0 = 8481, 6732 and 5678 km at 0.60, 1.20 and 2.00 M☉.
  • Ultra-relativistic: E = (C3 − C2)/R, no minimum. Positive means expand, negative means collapse.
  • C3/C2 = 1 at 1.72 M☉ (this model); about 1.4 M☉ in the exact calculation.

Common mix-ups

  • "A heavier white dwarf is larger." R0 ∝ M−1/3: from 0.60 to 1.20 M☉ it falls from 8481 to 6732 km.
  • "The ultra-relativistic star also sits at a minimum." Both terms go as 1/R, so there is no lowest point.
  • "1.44 and 1.72 disagree." They are different models: uniform sphere, np = 3 polytrope.
  • "At the minimum the kinetic energy equals the gravitational energy." Here 2EK + Egrav = 0, so the ratio reads 0.5000.

Things to try on your own

  • Non-relativistic at 1.00 M☉: R should read 7153 km and the mean kinetic energy 116.3 keV.
  • Ultra-relativistic at 1.50 M☉: the ratio should read 1.0952; at 1.80 M☉, 0.9699, below 1.
